chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Statistical Toolkit for Spotting Reversion

lessons.title: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Process: The Math Behind Reversion Speed

children.text: Everything in Lesson 6 was built one trading day at a time: yesterday's deviation, today's deviation, a slope called phi, a half-life measured in whole days. That is fine if you only ever look at daily closing prices. The moment you want to compare a strategy tested on daily data with one tested on hourly data, or put a theoretical, rather than arbitrary, band around your z-score thresholds, the daily step size gets in the way. The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process is the continuous-time version of the exact same idea, and once you see it, Chapter 1's AR(1) equation and Lesson 6's half-life formula turn out to be a single special case of it.

body.text: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process describes a value that is continuously pulled toward a long-run mean at a speed set by a single parameter, theta, while being continuously jolted by random noise. It is the mathematical object underneath every "mean reversion speed" number you will estimate in this course, whether you ever write out its full equation or not.

body.caption: theta is the speed of mean reversion, mu is the long-run mean, sigma is the volatility of the random shocks, and dW_t is an increment of a Wiener process (Brownian motion), the continuous-time analog of a random walk's step.

markDefs.definition: A continuous-time random process with independent, normally distributed increments. It is the mathematical foundation of continuous-time models of price randomness, playing the same role dW_t plays here that a coin flip played in Lesson 3's discrete random walk.

children.text: Read the equation as two forces added together at every instant. The first term, theta times (mu minus X_t), is a pull: whenever X_t is above mu, this term is negative and pushes it back down, whenever X_t is below mu, it is positive and pushes it back up, and the size of the push scales with how far away X_t currently is. This is the exact same idea as phi times the deviation in Chapter 1's AR(1) equation, just written to act continuously instead of once per day. The second term, sigma times

, is the random shock, unpredictable, mean-zero noise arriving continuously. Set theta to zero and the pull disappears entirely, leaving pure Brownian motion, the continuous-time random walk from Lesson 3 with no home to return to.

body.title: Fast vs slow mean reversion speed, same mean, different theta (illustrative simulation)

children.text: Connecting Theta to the Half-Life You Already Know

Sample an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process once every trading day and it turns out to look exactly like the AR(1) equation from Chapter 1, with phi equal to e raised to the power of minus theta times the time step. With a daily time step, that simplifies to phi equals e to the power of minus theta, or equivalently theta equals minus the natural log of phi. Take Lesson 6's example: a stock with an estimated phi of 0.85 has theta equal to minus ln(0.85), which is 0.1625 per day.

body.caption: The continuous-time half-life formula. It is algebraically the same statement as Lesson 6's minus ln(2) over ln(phi), just expressed in theta instead of phi.

body.label: Cross-check against Lesson 6
body.context: theta = -ln(0.85) = 0.1625 per day. Half-life = ln(2) / 0.1625 = 4.27 days, matching the 4.3-day estimate from Lesson 6's table for phi = 0.85. Same reversion speed, two equivalent ways of writing it down.

children.text: Two practical reasons. First, theta is expressed per unit of time, per day, per year, whichever you choose, rather than per data point, so a reversion speed estimated from daily closes and one estimated from hourly bars can be compared on the same footing once you convert both to the same time unit. Second, the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process has a known equilibrium distribution: left to run for long enough with theta, mu, and sigma held fixed, X_t settles into a normal distribution centered on mu with a specific, calculable variance. That gives you a theoretically grounded way to size a z-score threshold, instead of picking plus or minus 2 purely by convention, you can ask what deviation size is genuinely rare given this specific stock's own theta and sigma.

body.caption: The equilibrium (stationary) standard deviation implied by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process's own theta and sigma, a theoretically derived alternative to the rolling standard deviation used in Lesson 5's z-score.

body.text: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model assumes theta, mu, and sigma stay fixed forever, and that the random shocks are normally distributed. Neither assumption survives contact with real Indian equity markets for long. A stock's reversion speed and volatility can shift after a change in float, a sector re-rating, or the kind of structural break covered in Lesson 3 and Chapter 8, and Lesson 5 already flagged that real returns have fatter tails than a normal distribution allows for. Treat theta, mu, and sigma as estimates that need periodic re-fitting on a rolling window, never as fixed constants of nature for a given stock.

children.text: Fitting an OU Process in Python
Unlike Lesson 6's already-demeaned deviation series, here the regression runs on the raw level series itself, including an intercept, which lets you recover phi, theta, and mu in one step.

body.code:
import numpy as np

# 'spread' is the raw series (a price, or a price minus a reference
# level), NOT pre-centered around its own mean.
x = spread.shift(1).dropna()
y = spread.loc[x.index]

phi, c = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)   # phi = slope, c = intercept
dt = 1  # one trading day

theta = -np.log(phi) / dt
mu = c / (1 - phi)
half_life = np.log(2) / theta

print(f"theta = {theta:.4f} per day, mu = {mu:.2f}, half-life = {half_life:.1f} days")
body.caption: Recovering theta, mu, and half-life from an AR(1) fit on the raw (non-demeaned) series.

body.title: Compute the equilibrium standard deviation
body.prompt: A spread has an estimated theta of 0.15 per day and a residual volatility (sigma) of ₹2 per square root of a day. What is its equilibrium (stationary) standard deviation, in rupees, rounded to two decimal places?
body.explanation: SD = sigma / sqrt(2 x theta) = 2 / sqrt(0.30) = 2 / 0.5477 = 3.65. This is the theoretically implied "typical" size of a deviation once the process has settled into its equilibrium behavior, and can be used as a more principled alternative to an arbitrarily chosen rolling standard deviation.

body.title: Reading theta correctly
body.question: Stock X has an estimated theta of 0.35 per day. Stock Y has an estimated theta of 0.03 per day. Which statement is correct?
options: Stock X reverts faster, since a higher theta means a stronger pull back toward the mean at every instant
Stock Y reverts faster, since a lower theta means less resistance to movement
Theta has no relationship to reversion speed, only phi does
Both stocks revert at the same speed since theta only affects volatility, not speed
body.explanation: Theta is literally the speed-of-reversion parameter in the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck equation: a larger theta means a stronger pull back toward mu at every instant, and therefore a shorter half-life. Stock X's theta of 0.35 corresponds to a half-life of about 2 days, while Stock Y's theta of 0.03 corresponds to a half-life of over 23 days.

cards.definition: A continuous-time stochastic process that is pulled toward a long-run mean at a rate set by a mean-reversion speed parameter, theta, while being continuously perturbed by random noise.
The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck parameter controlling how strongly a process is pulled back toward its mean per unit time. Related to the discrete AR(1) coefficient phi by phi = e^(-theta x dt).
A continuous-time random process with independent, normally distributed increments, the continuous-time analog of a discrete random walk's coin-flip steps.
The long-run probability distribution an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process settles into if its parameters stay fixed, a normal distribution centered on mu with variance sigma squared divided by two theta.

points: The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process is the continuous-time version of the AR(1) equation from Chapter 1: a pull toward a mean at a rate theta, plus continuous random noise.
Theta and phi describe the same reversion speed in two equivalent languages: phi = e^(-theta x dt), so theta = -ln(phi) / dt when sampling daily.
Half-life can be written as ln(2) / theta, which gives the identical answer to Lesson 6's minus ln(2) / ln(phi) formula, just in a different but equivalent form.

The process's known equilibrium distribution gives a theoretically grounded standard deviation, sigma / sqrt(2 x theta), as an alternative to an arbitrarily chosen rolling standard deviation for setting z-score thresholds.
Theta, mu, and sigma are estimates, not fixed constants. They must be re-fit periodically, since a structural break can change all three without warning.
